metadata.title: Can AI Help Us Build Buildings That Use Less Energy?
metadata.audience: students: smart people getting started with AI
metadata.script_source: user-supplied script, lightly tightened to stay under 3:00 (user allowed edits)
metadata.structure_note: Script is the narration; composer cold open and hesitant-writer overview omitted to stay under 3:00. Closing question = Your Turn beat.

beats.narration_text: Imagine designing a building before a single brick is laid. What if you could test hundreds of versions of it, changing its orientation, windows, materials, insulation, airflow and shading, and find one that stays comfortable while using far less energy? And what if AI could help you do that?

show.event: a grid of building variants fills in

beats.narration_text: Buildings use enormous amounts of energy, for heating, cooling, lighting, ventilation and appliances. But a building's energy performance is decided long before anyone switches on a light. It starts with design.

show.event: design → construction → daily use; design ringed

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: the energy uses land first, the design timeline lands at the second sentence

beats.narration_text: How much sunlight does the building get? How much heat comes in through the windows? How well does it hold heat in winter? Could natural airflow replace some mechanical cooling? These are problems of physics and engineering.

show.event: four question cards land one by one

beats.narration_text: Take one example: heat transfer. Heat moves in three ways. Conduction, through solid materials. Convection, through moving air. And radiation, straight from the sun.

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: one card per mode of heat transfer, landing as each is named

beats.narration_text: Poor insulation lets heat escape in winter and sneak in during summer. Large windows bring daylight, but also unwanted heat. And a building's orientation changes how much sun reaches it through the day.

Engineers have long used energy simulations to weigh these factors. Now imagine combining building models, weather data, material properties and occupancy patterns with those simulations, and with AI.

AI could explore thousands of design combinations. It might find a better window-to-wall ratio, recommend shading, compare insulation materials, and predict energy demand before construction even begins.

show.event: cloud of design dots on energy vs comfort

beats.narration_text: Once the building is running, sensors track temperature, occupancy, humidity and energy use. AI can then adjust heating and cooling to actual conditions, instead of running systems at fixed settings.

show.event: fixed setting line vs AI line that follows occupancy

beats.narration_text: The goal isn't a building that uses more technology. It's a building that uses less energy to give the same comfort.
A truly sustainable building isn't just about what we add to it. Sometimes it's about what we remove: wasted energy, heat loss, inefficient systems, and poor design decisions.

show.event: four chips of waste land, then dim

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: the waste chips land as named, then dim, then the closing line lands

beats.narration_text: So here's a question: If we could redesign every building around climate, energy and human comfort, would we still build the way we do today?
